lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the Indian firm
lead.head: One firm, a hundred Indias

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 37

body: Amit Varma opened by promis­ing to talk about “the bor­ing sub­ject of Bollywood”, while Ajay Shah took the Indian busi­ness land­scape and the next 20 years. {037-J01}

It turned out to be one con­ver­sa­tion. Varma’s first clip, a song from *Baazigar*, was read with mock grav­ity as a dis­ser­ta­tion on why local knowl­edge beats book­ish knowl­edge. That was Shah’s theme too.

His story of the Indian firm ran in three acts. In the first, firms were na­tional only in name. In the sec­ond, tech­nol­ogy made them truly na­tional. In the third, still to come, they must learn to be local again.
## Out of headquarters’ reach

Until the 1980s, Shah said, a firm could op­er­ate all over India while its branch man­agers did their own thing. They had to be em­pow­ered, be­cause they had no way to check back with head­quar­ters.

That al­lowed sen­si­ble local adap­ta­tion, but also sloppy process and petty cor­rup­tion. Shah bor­rowed Lant Pritchett’s image of the Indian state[[x1]]: a brain whose nerves to the fin­gers have been sev­ered.
From the 1990s, com­put­ers and, above all, tele­com ended that. For the first time, Indian firms had cen­tral in­for­ma­tion, cen­tral process de­sign and op­er­a­tional con­trols. {037-C01}
Shah counts this as an en­gine of the GDP ex­plo­sion from 1991 to 2011: firms grew in scale and pro­duc­tiv­ity with­out adding much labour. Few peo­ple, he said, have re­marked on it.
## The great flat­ten­ing
Success brought its own trap. Firms came to be­lieve in one firm, one list of prod­ucts and one process de­sign, rolled out all across India.
India is too di­verse for that, Shah ar­gued. He prefers the map drawn from CMIE’s house­hold data: about 100 ho­mo­ge­neous re­gions, each a clus­ter of about seven dis­tricts within one state.
Measured that way, he said, India is more di­verse than Europe or Africa. {037-C05}

Global firms al­ready be­have ac­cord­ingly. Nestle tunes Maggi for each coun­try. Why, Shah asked, should one Maggi, or one home-loan al­go­rithm, serve all of India? “That re­ally seems pre­pos­ter­ous given the amount of di­ver­sity of India,” he said. {037-C06}

Varma pushed back: Amazon and YouTube al­ready cater to a mar­ket of one. Shah replied that every per­sonal pre­dic­tion comes from a model fit­ted to a pool of peo­ple. The real de­ci­sion is which pool.
## A trea­sury at the top

Shah’s pre­scrip­tion bor­rows from multi­na­tion­als, which know Poland is dif­fer­ent from France. Headquarters keeps strat­egy, cap­i­tal, gov­er­nance and the board. Regional units run their own profit and loss, adapt their prod­ucts and mod­els, and bid for cap­i­tal. {037-C09}

“It is easy to be a sim­ple Stalinist cen­tralised firm rolling out ev­ery­thing all across the coun­try,” he said. The adap­tive firm is harder. But the na­tional gi­ants, for all their tril­lion-rupee val­u­a­tions, have only scratched the sur­face of the Indian mar­ket.
Some, he ex­pects, will learn to make their ar­mour more flex­i­ble. The rest leave space for local firms.
Varma saw the shape of the whole: firms local be­cause they had to be, then cen­tralised by tech­nol­ogy, com­ing full cir­cle to local again.
He also had a com­pli­ment ready. India, he often says, in­hab­its three cen­turies at once. Shah’s mind, he added, is in the 22nd.

second.label: Taste of the market
second.head: Maggi with a passport
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why Maggi and Kit Kat taste different in every country

pic.caption: A Kit Kat chocolate bar split in half

body: Buy Maggi noo­dles in Indonesia, India and the UK, Ajay Shah said, and you will find they all taste dif­fer­ent. Nestle runs focus groups and re­search to find the right flavour for Thailand, Indonesia or India. {037-S04}

Kit Kat varies too[[x2]]. Fans re­vere the British orig­i­nal. Americans, Shah said, are stuck with a sugar-loaded ver­sion pushed by Hershey’s, and trav­ellers to Japan carry bag­fuls home. His ad­vice: buy both in every coun­try you visit. “It’s great fun.”

Then he turned the les­son on India. Would Tamilians and Punjabis eat the same Maggi? As India’s mar­ket ap­proaches the size of an Indonesia or a Thailand, he ar­gued, one prod­uct for the whole coun­try stops mak­ing sense. {037-C06}

quote.text: The orig­i­nal British Kit Kat is per­fect. Kit Kats in Japan are mag­i­cal. Kit Kat in America are hor­ri­ble.

third.head: The phone in her hand

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on women and mobile phones

body: For the de­cen­tral­i­sa­tion chap­ter of *In Service of the Republic*, his book with Vijay Kelkar, Ajay Shah lined up CMIE’s 100 ho­mo­ge­neous re­gions[[x3]] and com­pared the rich­est with the poor­est. {037-S06}
The rich­est, he found, is about 5.3 times richer than the poor­est. That was “a nice num­ber to know”, he said, but not the one that stuck in his head.
The one that stuck was the share of women who own a mo­bile phone. It re­flects a household’s pros­per­ity, but also its so­cial pro­gres­siv­ity: whether it will give a teenage girl a phone at all.
In the top re­gions the share is about 18 times higher than in the bot­tom ones. “That’s huge lev­els of vari­a­tion,” Shah said. {#eighteen}

p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s case that Indian firms, having learnt to be national, must now learn to be local again

quote.text: There is a brain, but the nerves have been sev­ered and the fin­gers are doing their own thing.

photo.caption: Ronald Coase in 2003
photo.credit: University of Chicago Law School, Attribution

box.title: The paper behind the question
box.text: Ronald Coase’s *The Nature of the Firm*[[x7]][[x8]] asked why firms are run cen­trally in­side while mar­kets out­side run on con­tracts and prices. Ajay Shah took it as his start­ing point for ask­ing whether firms need so much cen­tral con­trol in­side. {037-C10}

sections.label: The first age
sections.head: When the branch was a kingdom
sections.caption: the old Indian firm
body: In the bad old days, Ajay Shah said, you could build a firm that op­er­ated all over India, but its op­er­a­tional con­trols were very weak. Branch man­agers had to be em­pow­ered, be­cause there was no way for them to check back with head­quar­ters. {037-S01}

“I al­ways like to re­mind ev­ery­body that Robert Clive did his own thing be­cause there was no email,” he said. Indian branch man­agers were much the same: they had con­sid­er­able dis­cre­tion, and cus­tomers knew it was worth ar­gu­ing with them. {037-S02}
Amit Varma saw a fea­ture as well as a bug. Being in Patiala or in Patna makes a ma­te­rial dif­fer­ence to the ap­proach you take with a cus­tomer, he said.
## A brain with­out nerves
The bug, Shah said, was process fail­ure. Different peo­ple were idio­syn­cratic and did their own thing, and petty cor­rup­tion crept in.

He bor­rowed Lant Pritchett’s de­scrip­tion of the Indian state: a brain whose nerves have been sev­ered, with the fin­gers doing their own thing. Every large firm be­came “a coali­tion of var­i­ous in­di­vid­u­als doing their own thing”, un­able to hold to a strat­egy or man­age risk. {037-C02}
Shah said he was not there to ven­er­ate that era, only to de­scribe it. We have for­got­ten these things, he said, and think of them as pre­his­tory.
~ Varma marked the mo­ment with a clip from *Gangs of Wasseypur Part 2*, stand­ing for headquarters’ dis­dain for a local man­ager who doesn’t get it. {037-J10}

quote.text: There is a brain, but the nerves have been sev­ered and the fin­gers are doing their own thing.

sections.label: The second age
sections.head: Clive gets email
sections.caption: the true national firm
body: From the 1990s, Ajay Shah said, Indian firms got com­put­ers and, more im­por­tantly, tele­com. Early VSAT links came in the late 1990s, and se­ri­ous in­ter­net con­nec­tiv­ity in the 2000s. {#vsat}

Firms now had cen­tralised in­for­ma­tion, cen­tralised process de­sign and op­er­a­tional con­trols. Robert Clive was no longer a loose can­non far away. “Now Robert Clive was under the daily mis­ery of sur­veil­lance from HQ,” Shah said. {037-C01}
## The en­gine no­body no­ticed

Shah counts this as one of the great de­vel­op­ments of the Indian econ­omy, a piece of the GDP ex­plo­sion from 1991 to 2011. {#gdp} Andersen Consulting, now Accenture, helped spread process en­gi­neer­ing and ERP sys­tems across hun­dreds of firms, which grew in scale with­out adding much labour.

Until then, he said, tele­com had been the choke point, ei­ther un­avail­able or priced “out­right crazy”. In the Vajpayee years, Sudheendra Kulkarni and N.K. Singh[[x10]] “did amaz­ing things” and blew up the Department of Telecom’s “death grip”[[x9]]. {037-J13}

Amit Varma won­dered how much came from im­ported ideas, with the dan­ger of iso­mor­phic mimicry. Shah said the chan­nel was less the busi­ness schools than the prac­tices of global firms: in bank­ing, through for­eign banks and peo­ple who had worked in them. {037-C04}
~ Shah ad­mires that work. But, he warned, it came with a dif­fi­culty of its own.

quote.text: This is the heart, the en­gine of how so­phis­ti­cated scale and pro­duc­tiv­ity emerged in Indian cap­i­tal­ism.

sections.label: The catch
sections.head: More diverse than a continent
sections.caption: India’s hundred regions
body: The dif­fi­culty, Ajay Shah said, was ex­ces­sive cen­tral­i­sa­tion. Firms got “drugged” on the idea of one firm, one list of prod­ucts and one process de­sign, rolled out across all of India, flat­ten­ing the country’s rich­ness and com­plex­ity.

His al­ter­na­tive map comes from CMIE’s house­hold data, which di­vides India into about 100 ho­mo­ge­neous re­gions. Each is a con­tigu­ous group of dis­tricts within one state, with sim­i­lar women’s lit­er­acy and a sim­i­lar agro­cli­matic zone. After more than 10 years, he is “a great en­thu­si­ast”. {037-R12}
With India at 140 crore peo­ple, that is about 14 mil­lion peo­ple per re­gion, or seven dis­tricts on av­er­age. {#fourteen}
## Borders by ac­ci­dent
Nor should a firm think in states. “Like re­ally should UP be one state? Okay, it makes no sense,” Shah said. {037-J05}

Measured re­gion by re­gion, India is more di­verse than Europe or Africa, he ar­gued. Lant Pritchett once told him[[x11]] that by some mea­sures India’s gap be­tween top and bot­tom is wider than that of Latin America and Africa merged, which would mean re­vers­ing ge­o­log­i­cal drift. {037-C05}
~ So why, Shah asked, should a lender’s soft­ware use the iden­ti­cal home-loan al­go­rithm in every cor­ner of the coun­try? {037-C06}

quote.text: Don’t even think of India as a bunch of states be­cause the state bound­aries are kinda ran­dom.

sections.label: The pushback
sections.head: A data set of one won’t do
sections.caption: the market of one
body: Amit Varma was not con­vinced by the 100 re­gions. With 1.4 bil­lion Indians, he said, there are in a sense 1.4 bil­lion ho­mo­ge­neous re­gions, and tech­nol­ogy al­ready caters to each. His Amazon al­go­rithm does not show him what it shows some­body else in Mumbai.
Ajay Shah replied that the un­der­ly­ing code could still dif­fer by coun­try. Somebody is es­ti­mat­ing a model, and that model can work at dif­fer­ent lev­els of ab­strac­tion.
## The pool­ing ques­tion

His ex­am­ple was the credit card de­fault pre­dic­tion model, “the en­gine in­side every fi­nan­cial firm that is­sues a credit card”. {#creditcard} A pre­dic­tion for one cus­tomer still needs data pooled across many. {037-C07} Which pool, the world, India, South India, Tamil Nadu or one re­gion, is “the de­ci­sion box”.
If farm­ers kill them­selves in Marathwada, Shah said, that shapes his think­ing about the model for Marathwada dif­fer­ently. {#marathwada}

Varma brought in Rahul Matthan’s *The Third Way*: lenders now judge cred­it­wor­thi­ness by whether you type in all caps, or whether you let your phone bat­tery[[x12]] run down to 3 or 4 per cent. {037-S09}
~ Varma con­ceded the point for the real world. Nestle, he said, can­not make 1.4 bil­lion Maggi flavours, even if his YouTube feed is his alone.

quote.text: You can’t make a pre­dic­tion for a cus­tomer of one with a data set of one.

sections.label: The fix
sections.head: Poland is not France
sections.caption: the federated firm
body: How should a firm re­design it­self to serve many Indias? The an­swers, Ajay Shah said, are “ac­tu­ally not that hard”: imag­ine you were a com­pany op­er­at­ing in 20 coun­tries.

Every global cor­po­ra­tion knows that Poland is dif­fer­ent from France, he said. {#poland} Their of­fer­ings com­bine the cen­tral and the local: some things are done dif­fer­ently for Poland, some dif­fer­ently for France. Indian firms can bor­row that knowl­edge and doc­trine.
## A fed­er­a­tion of mini CEOs

The core would be a head­quar­ters for strat­egy, cap­i­tal al­lo­ca­tion, gov­er­nance, the board and HR. Around it would sit a fed­er­ated, de­cen­tralised ar­chi­tec­ture of busi­ness groups, each in charge of its own profit and loss. The one sent to con­quer UP and Bihar would be “like a mini CEO”, with con­sid­er­able free­dom.
Later he sharp­ened the idea. Headquarters would be the trea­sury, and re­gional units would bid for its cap­i­tal, com­pet­ing with one an­other on re­turn on eq­uity. {037-C09}

Firms can sit any­where on a spec­trum. At one end is Casio, which says, in Shah’s car­i­ca­ture: “This is my watch, hell with you, I’m just sell­ing this watch.” Only its ad­ver­tis­ing and dis­tri­bu­tion change. {#casio}
~ At the other end, prod­uct, process and ser­vice grow ever more flex­i­ble. Those are the trade-offs, Shah said, that man­agers will need to ad­dress in India in com­ing years.

quote.text: The var­i­ous sub firms all over India should be in an auc­tion where they ask for cap­i­tal and then they use it ef­fi­ciently.

sections.label: The rethink
sections.head: Seeing like a firm
sections.caption: the blind national firm
body: Amit Varma asked how much large firms could mimic the bot­tom-up pro­cesses that work so well in so­ci­ety.

Ajay Shah began with Ronald Coase, who first asked why firms run on cen­tral com­mand in­side while the world out­side runs on con­tracts and prices. Today, Shah said, we can ask: “Do you re­ally need to be that Stalinist?” {037-C10}
## The blind giant

James C Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*[[x13]][[x14]] de­scribes states un­able to per­ceive ground re­al­ity. Big na­tional firms, Shah ar­gued, share the blind­ness. They serve one slice of the in­come dis­tri­bu­tion in each re­gion and leave large parts of the coun­try un­served. {037-C08}
That leaves room for local firms, like the deeply op­ti­mised Rajasthan firm, even though no­body can match the na­tional firms’ cost of cap­i­tal.

His test is to com­pute rev­enue, profit or re­turn on eq­uity in each ho­mo­ge­neous re­gion. If the num­bers are widely dis­persed, he said, “to some ex­tent I’ll turn around and blame the firm.” {037-C12}
Serving the weak­est re­gions, where peo­ple have some dis­pos­able in­come too, means get­ting off the high horse of one prod­uct for all India.
~ The case grows with the mar­ket. In 1991, Shah re­called, all of Bank of America’s Indian op­er­a­tions were like those in some small American state. {037-S07}

quote.text: But the ar­ro­gance of the big na­tional firm makes it blind. It makes it dif­fi­cult for the firm to see that re­al­ity.

portraits.caption: James C. Scott
portraits.credit: SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0

quote.text: All of us have lived it, we’ve just stopped notic­ing it, and I want to pull this out of our con­scious­ness and say that this was big, this was huge.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: From an airline counter to Nehru’s jail, four tales and their lessons

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on where power sat in the old Indian firm
stories.head: The demigod behind the desk
body: Picture a cus­tomer, in the days be­fore the 1990s, ar­gu­ing with an Indian Airlines front­line em­ployee: earnestly, sin­cerely, plead­ing, “Do some­thing for me.” For Ajay Shah, that scene sums up the old Indian firm. {037-S02}

The cus­tomer was not wast­ing breath. “Actually, the front­line em­ploy­ees of Indian Airlines had[[x15]] a lot of dis­cre­tion,” Shah said. “They could do many things. They were se­ri­ously pow­er­ful peo­ple.”

Banks worked the same way. The teller was rea­son­ably dis­em­pow­ered. But the branch man­ager “was like a demigod”, with se­ri­ous dis­cre­tion over gen­uinely im­por­tant de­ci­sions, and that made it worth your while ar­gu­ing with him.

The rea­son was tech­nol­ogy. A firm could op­er­ate all over India, but with no way for man­agers to check back with head­quar­ters, they had to be em­pow­ered. Robert Clive, as Shah likes to re­mind ev­ery­body, did his own thing be­cause there was no email. {037-S01}
So power sat at the local front line. Staff thought for them­selves and evolved the of­fer­ing in ways that made sense, and also in­dulged their own petty bi­ases and local cor­rup­tion.
Computers and tele­com would later drain that dis­cre­tion away to head­quar­ters.

~ Amit Varma heard in this the an­swer to a puz­zle. Working at a Starbucks, he had over­heard a woman lose her tem­per with Amazon cus­tomer care and vow never to buy from the com­pany again. The agent was a call-centre worker with a script, who could not help her. “But this kind of ex­plains why that habit would have been there,” Varma said. {037-S03}
stories.why: Whom cus­tomers bother to per­suade shows where power sits in an or­gan­i­sa­tion. And habits out­live the de­sign that formed them: peo­ple still argue with front­line staff who no longer have any dis­cre­tion.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Indian Airlines employee

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on CMIE’s map of a southern state
stories.head: Kerala in three, not ten
body: CMIE’s al­go­rithm groups India’s roughly 700 dis­tricts into about 100 ho­mo­ge­neous re­gions[[x16]]. {#districts} Ajay Shah’s sim­ple ex­am­ple is Kerala, which comes out as three. {037-S05}
“There’s North Kerala, there’s cen­tral Kerala, and there’s South Kerala,” he said.

He has dis­cussed the find­ing with many peo­ple who know the state, and their ver­dict was: this makes sense. Kerala is ac­tu­ally quite di­verse. The north dif­fers from the mid­dle, and the mid­dle from the south, in in­ter­est­ing and im­por­tant ways.

~ Just as im­por­tant, three is the right level of ab­strac­tion. You do not want to go to ten. A good map, in Shah’s telling, is fine enough to show real dif­fer­ences and sim­ple enough to stay use­ful.

quote.text: Kerala is about three pieces and you should think about them dif­fer­ently.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the three Keralas

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on firms that will not go north
stories.head: Mutter curses, miss markets
body: Ajay Shah knows some firms that are in their com­fort zone play­ing South India. Ask them about the North and they will mut­ter strange curses. {037-S08}
North India, they say, is some waste­land: they don’t know how to op­er­ate there, and they won’t. You could be­have like that, Shah said.

His ad­vice is to hire some “red-blooded North Indians” and fig­ure out how to play in that mar­ket, be­cause there is some up­side there. The tidy, calm ways of op­er­at­ing in the south won’t work there, he said. Working out what will is the firm’s job.
~ Amit Varma ob­jected to the phrase. “Everyone is red-blooded,” he said. “I did not ex­pect the sad stereo­typ­ing from you.” {037-J06}
stories.why: When a firm calls a mar­ket too dif­fi­cult, Shah sug­gested, it is often de­scrib­ing the lim­its of its own un­der­stand­ing. A wide gap in prof­its be­tween re­gions points to a fail­ure of the firm, not the mar­ket. {037-C12}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on firms that shun the North

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the book he understood only as an adult
stories.head: History, from memory
body: Ajay Shah’s rec­om­men­da­tion was a book most Indians meet in child­hood: Jawaharlal Nehru’s *The Discovery of India*[[x17]]. He read it at 12 or so, and woke up to it only slowly. {#twelve}
Rereading it as a grown-up a cou­ple of years ago, he found it “lit­er­ally the book that in­vents the idea of India”. {037-R07}

Amit Varma asked whether Nehru had writ­ten it in prison, with the quotes and ref­er­ences from mem­ory. He was in jail, Shah said, but po­lit­i­cal pris­on­ers were treated well and he was given ac­cess to books. He had no li­brary and no com­puter, only a cou­ple of books on his desk that friends ro­tated. {037-S10}
~ *Glimpses of World History*[[x18]], his let­ters to Indira Gandhi, was also done from mem­ory. Varma’s ver­dict: “He would have been a pod­caster today.” {037-J09}
stories.why: These found­ing books came out of what one mind could hold. Shah urges adults who read *The Discovery of India* as chil­dren to go back to it; Varma urges chil­dren to read it now.

quiz.q: How many homogeneous regions does Kerala split into on CMIE’s map, and what are they?
quiz.a: Three: North, cen­tral and South Kerala; Shah says three, not ten, is right.

quiz.q: Which single statistic about women stayed in Ajay Shah’s head from the regional data?
quiz.a: The share of women own­ing a mo­bile phone, about 18 times higher at the top.

quiz.q: Which credit-scoring signals did Amit Varma cite from his conversation with Rahul Matthan?
quiz.a: Whether you type in all caps, and how low you let your phone bat­tery run.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s federated firm, what role does headquarters play for the regional units?
quiz.a: It acts as trea­sury; re­gions bid for cap­i­tal and com­pete on re­turn on eq­uity.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 37. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Robert Clive (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Ronald Coase (University of Chicago Law School, Attribution); Kit Kat (Evan-Amos, public domain); James C. Scott (SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Apple.

shelf.title: Desperately Seeking Shah Rukh
shelf.creator: Shrayana Bhattacharya
shelf.why: Shrayana Bhattacharya uses Indian women’s ado­ra­tion of Shah Rukh Khan as a lens on Indian so­ci­ety and how lonely its women are; Amit says it ‘con­tains multitudes’, from eco­nom­ics and so­ci­ol­ogy to beau­ti­ful writ­ing.

shelf.title: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shrayana Bhattacharya
shelf.why: Amit’s most pop­u­lar Seen and the Unseen episode, a con­ver­sa­tion with Shrayana Bhattacharya (who gave him the ‘anti-uncle’ label) on the eco­nomic and so­cial lives of Indian women.

shelf.title: Vivian Gornick’s books
shelf.creator: Vivian Gornick
shelf.why: He calls Gornick ‘the great memoirist’ and says all of her books are rec­om­men­da­tions.

shelf.title: The Loneliness of the Indian Man (Episode 303, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Nikhil Taneja
shelf.why: More than seven hours with Nikhil Taneja on the male side of the gen­der di­vide: half the coun­try can’t talk to the other half.

shelf.title: The Loneliness of the Long-Distance Runner
shelf.creator: Alan Sillitoe
shelf.why: He calls it Sillitoe’s ‘great novel’.

shelf.title: The Loneliness of the Long-Distance Trucker (Episode 192, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Rajat Ubhaykar
shelf.why: It is a con­ver­sa­tion with Rajat Ubhaykar, who wrote a book about truck­ing across India.

shelf.title: The Discovery of India
shelf.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
shelf.why: The book Ajay calls ‘lit­er­ally the book that in­vents the idea of India’: an idea grounded in his­tory and free of ha­tred, in a mod­ern syn­the­sis com­fort­able with sci­ence and lib­eral democ­racy.

shelf.title: Glimpses of World History
shelf.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
shelf.why: Nehru’s let­ters to his daugh­ter Indira, a his­tory of the world writ­ten from prison largely from mem­ory.

shelf.title: Is India a Flailing State?
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett
shelf.why: Pritchett’s image of the Indian state as a world-class brain of se­nior of­fi­cials whose nerves to the limbs are cut, so noth­ing changes on the ground.

shelf.title: The Nature of the Firm
shelf.creator: Ronald Coase
shelf.why: Coase’s an­swer to why firms exist when mar­kets can co­or­di­nate through prices: con­tract­ing is costly.

shelf.title: Seeing Like a State
shelf.creator: James C Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how state schemes to im­prove the human con­di­tion fail when bu­reau­cra­cies can­not ‘see’ the so­ci­ety they rule, with a tool­kit (state leg­i­bil­ity, high mod­ernism, metis) you can apply al­most any­where.

shelf.title: CMIE household data (Consumer Pyramids)
shelf.creator: CMIE / Mahesh Vyas
shelf.why: CMIE’s house­hold sur­vey (about 190,000 house­holds, three times a year, across some 100 ho­mo­ge­neous re­gions) makes India’s di­ver­sity mea­sur­able, from five­fold in­come gaps be­tween re­gions to how many house­holds re­ally live off farm­ing.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Buying Maggi noodles and Kit Kats in every country you visit
shelf.why: ‘It’s great fun.’ You taste first-hand how firms tai­lor one prod­uct to local pref­er­ences.

shelf.title: The Reason British Kit Kats Taste Better Than America’s
shelf.creator: Gregory Lovvorn
shelf.why: Background on why the British Kit Kat that fans re­vere dif­fers from the American one.

shelf.title: Japanese Kit Kat Flavours: The Complete List
shelf.why: It shows how far one brand will go to lo­calise for a sin­gle mar­ket.

shelf.title: Rahul Matthan Seeks the Protocol (Episode 360, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Rahul Matthan
shelf.why: Rahul Matthan makes the strong­est case that Aadhaar has pri­vacy built into its de­sign, the view Ajay chal­lenges.

shelf.title: The Third Way
shelf.creator: Rahul Matthan
shelf.why: Its dis­cus­sion of credit de­ci­sions tai­lored to in­di­vid­u­als with big data.

shelf.title: A Venture Capitalist Looks at the World (Episode 213, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Sajith Pai
shelf.why: Pai ar­gues the Indian mar­ket is far smaller than its 1.4 bil­lion head­count sug­gests.

shelf.title: The Indus Valley Playbook
shelf.creator: Sajith Pai
shelf.why: It di­vides Indians by in­come into a small af­flu­ent top, a mid­dle class with mid­dle-income-country lives, and a large base liv­ing like sub-Saharan Africa.

shelf.title: How Family Firms Evolve (Episode 34, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Original think­ing from Ajay on how Indian firms evolved over 30 years and how they should ma­ture: from fam­ily con­trol to dis­persed share­hold­ing, a pow­er­ful board and a man­age­ment team ac­count­able to it.

shelf.title: Kitaben Bahut Si (Baazigar)
shelf.creator: Zafar Gorakhpuri (lyricist)
shelf.why: Amit reads the lyrics, with mock se­ri­ous­ness, as an ar­gu­ment that book­ish knowl­edge and cre­den­tials mat­ter less than real, local knowl­edge, which is the theme of the episode.

shelf.title: Beta Tumse Na Ho Payega (Gangs of Wasseypur Part 2)
shelf.why: Amit’s Bollywood il­lus­tra­tion of the gap be­tween HQ and the field.

shelf.title: Sirf Ek Naam Sunayi Deta Hai (Chak De India)
shelf.why: The state-team cap­tain ver­sus na­tional coach clash an­tic­i­pates the shift from local satraps to one na­tional firm.

shelf.title: Main Aai Hoon U.P. Bihar Lootne (Shool)
shelf.why: A jok­ing nod to re­gion-specific strat­egy.

shelf.title: Ranbir Kapoor’s dialogue from Rocket Singh: Salesman of the Year
shelf.why: Introduced with the line ‘Bollywood has done in­terquar­tile range.

laughs.text: Amit’s open­ing: Ajay will cover the Indian busi­ness land­scape for the next 20 years (‘Terribly ex­cit­ing, isn’t it?’), while Amit will ‘talk about the bor­ing sub­ject of Bollywood.’ He then asks view­ers to pic­ture Ajay, in­stead of Shah Rukh Khan, jump­ing around and singing in Baazigar, and sug­gests they use good AI to make that clip.

Amit calls Baazigar lyri­cist Zafar Gorakhpuri ‘a great philoso­pher, and I’m say­ing this only on the basis of these words.’ He presents ‘Kitaben Bahut Si’ as a mag­nif­i­cent dis­ser­ta­tion couched in a song, prov­ing that book­ish knowl­edge is ir­rel­e­vant and cre­den­tial­ism is non­sense.
Amit: ‘I often say that India in­hab­its three cen­turies at the same time, 19th, 20th, 21st. But now I add a fourth to that list be­cause your mind is in the 22nd cen­tury.’
Ajay on India’s state bound­aries: ‘Like re­ally should UP be one state? Okay, it makes no sense.’
When Ajay sug­gests hir­ing ‘red-blooded North Indians’, Amit ob­jects: ‘Everyone is red-blooded… I did not ex­pect the sad stereo­typ­ing from you.’
After all the talk of vari­abil­ity and in­terquar­tile ranges, the Bollywood cue: ‘Bollywood has done in­terquar­tile range. Watch.’ A Ranbir Kapoor scene from Rocket Singh fol­lows.
On Amit’s run of ‘Loneliness of…’ episodes: ‘It should have been Lonely Reader.’ Amit con­cludes that he’s done with the se­ries be­cause we’re all lonely any­way.
On Nehru writ­ing his his­to­ries from mem­ory in prison with a few ro­tat­ing books, Amit says: ‘He would have been a pod­caster today.’
Gangs of Wasseypur Part 2’s ‘Beta tumse na ho payega’ scene, which Amit plays to de­pict HQ’s dis­dain for the local man­ager who ‘doesn’t get it’.
Chak De India’s ‘Sirf ek naam sunayi deta hai’ clash be­tween a state-team cap­tain and the coach of the Indian na­tional women’s team, used to set up the rise of the na­tional firm.
‘Main Aai Hoon U.P. Bihar Lootne’ from Shool, which Amit plays as a nod to re­gional strat­egy: ‘not quite’ hy­per­local, but ‘a step in the right di­rec­tion.’
Sudheendra Kulkarni and N.K. Singh, whom Ajay cred­its with ‘amaz­ing things’ in the Vajpayee years that ‘blew up the death grip of the de­part­ment of tele­com on Indian Telecom.’
Andersen Consulting, now Accenture, whose time-and-motion and en­ter­prise process en­gi­neer­ing Ajay says spread across hun­dreds of Indian firms.
Mahesh Vyas and CMIE, be­hind the al­go­rithm that di­vides India into about 100 ho­mo­ge­neous re­gions.
Alan Sillitoe’s The Loneliness of the Long-Distance Runner, the tem­plate for Amit’s Seen and the Unseen ti­tles: the Long-Distance Trucker, the Indian Woman and the Indian Man.
